The chairman of our residents' group does most of the work himself.
The chairman's report is reproduced in full in the appendix.

confusables.difference: Chair is the modern gender-neutral form and is now preferred in British writing: she chairs the committee, she is the chair.
A manager runs day-to-day work. A chairman leads a board or a meeting and usually is not an employee.

entry_json.avoid: Chairman is increasingly dated. In an IELTS essay, chair or chairperson is the safer choice.

entry_json.definition: something difficult that tests your ability, or an invitation to compete
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Feeding a growing population without more farmland is the real challenge.
example_sentences: Learning the alphabet again was the biggest challenge.
The job is a challenge, but I enjoy it.

contexts.text: The greatest challenge facing cities is not growth itself but growth without planning.
The biggest challenge was definitely the language at first.
Participants reported the timed section as the greatest challenge.

confusables.difference: A problem is negative and needs fixing. A challenge is difficult but implies it can be overcome, which is a more positive framing.
Difficulty is the abstract quality of being hard. A challenge is the specific task itself.

entry_json.avoid: Face or meet a challenge, not do a challenge. Beware of overusing challenge as a softer word for problem.

entry_json.definition: a person or team that has won a competition; also someone who publicly supports a cause
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The defending champion lost in the second round.
example_sentences: She was national champion three years running.
He became a champion of free access to museums.

contexts.text: Sporting champions are held up as role models long after their careers end.
My cousin was a regional swimming champion, which the family never stops mentioning.
The champion of the reform movement is described in chapter four.

confusables.difference: A winner won one particular event. A champion holds a title, usually across a season or competition.
The championship is the competition or the title. The champion is the person who holds it.

entry_json.avoid: A champion OF a cause, not a champion FOR one.

entry_json.definition: a television or radio station; also a passage for water, or a way of communicating
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are hundreds of channels and nothing worth watching.
example_sentences: Complaints should go through the proper channels.
The channel between the two islands is only a kilometre wide.

contexts.text: Social media has become the main channel through which young people encounter news.
I mostly watch one or two channels and stream everything else.
Complaints must be submitted through the official channels.

confusables.difference: In British English a radio station and a television channel. Do not swap the two nouns.
A canal is dug by people for boats. A channel is usually natural water between two areas of land.

entry_json.avoid: Through the proper channels is a fixed formal phrase, excellent in a complaint letter.

entry_json.definition: one of the parts a book is divided into; also a distinct period in a life or history
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first chapter explains the method in detail.
example_sentences: I read a chapter every night before I sleep.
Moving abroad opened a new chapter in her life.

contexts.text: Moving to another country opened a new chapter that I had not planned at all.
The opening chapter sets out the theoretical framework.
Textbooks divided into short chapters are read more often than dense ones.

confusables.difference: A section is any subdivision, including part of a chapter. A chapter is a major numbered division of a book.
Episodes belong to television series. Chapters belong to books.

entry_json.avoid: A new chapter in someone's life is a common and natural metaphor in Speaking Part 2.

entry_json.definition: a typical quality or feature of a person or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Patience is the characteristic most teachers say matters most.
example_sentences: The two species share several characteristics.
A defining characteristic of the city is how green it is.

contexts.text: The defining characteristic of a successful public space is that people stay in it without spending money.
The main characteristic of my home town is that everyone knows everyone.
Sample characteristics are summarised in Table 1.

confusables.difference: Feature is neutral and can be any noticeable part. A characteristic is typical of that thing and helps identify it.
Personality is the whole of who someone is. A characteristic is one trait within it.

entry_json.avoid: As an adjective it means typical: characteristic of the region. As a noun it needs a or the.

entry_json.definition: the amount of money asked for a service; also a formal accusation, or responsibility for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no charge for cancelling more than 24 hours in advance.
example_sentences: An additional charge applies for baggage.
She is in charge of the whole department.

contexts.text: Museums that make entry free of charge attract visitors who would never otherwise come.
I am in charge of the kitchen rota, which nobody envies.
Delivery is provided free of charge for orders over 30 pounds.

confusables.difference: Cost is what something is worth or takes to make. A charge is the specific amount a company asks you to pay.
You pay a price for goods and a charge for a service. A bank makes charges; a shop sets prices.

entry_json.avoid: Free of charge and in charge of are fixed. Do not write in the charge of when you mean responsible for.

entry_json.definition: to act dishonestly in order to gain an advantage, especially in a test or game
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Students who cheat in exams usually harm themselves most.
example_sentences: He was caught cheating in the final paper.
It is easy to cheat at online tests, which is the problem.

contexts.text: Online examinations are easy to cheat in, which is why so many institutions returned to invigilated halls.
Somebody in my class was caught cheating and was expelled.
Instances of cheating fell after the assessment format was changed.

confusables.difference: Copy describes the specific act of taking someone else's answers. Cheat is the general dishonesty, including using notes.
Plagiarism is presenting someone else's writing as your own. Cheating is broader and covers exams, games and sport.

entry_json.avoid: Cheat IN an exam but cheat AT a game. And cheat someone out of something means to swindle them.

entry_json.definition: happy and showing it, or making people feel happy
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The staff are always cheerful, even at seven in the morning.
example_sentences: She is remarkably cheerful for someone who works nights.
The room is bright and cheerful.

contexts.text: The driver was so cheerful that the whole bus ended up in a good mood.
I am not particularly cheerful before about ten in the morning.
A cheerful working environment is worth more to staff retention than a small pay rise.

confusables.difference: Happy is how you feel inside. Cheerful is how you appear to others, and suggests it is a habit rather than a mood.
Optimistic is about expecting good outcomes. Cheerful is about visible good mood now.

entry_json.avoid: Cheerful is spoken register and describes people and places. It suits Speaking Part 2 descriptions well.

entry_json.definition: a substance used in or produced by chemistry, especially a manufactured one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chemicals used on farmland end up in the rivers.
example_sentences: The factory releases several chemicals into the air.
This cleaner contains no harsh chemicals.

contexts.text: Agricultural chemicals raise yields in the short term and damage soil life over decades.
I try to use fewer chemicals at home, mostly for the sake of the cat.
Chemical concentrations were measured at three points along the river.

confusables.difference: Substance is any kind of material. A chemical is specifically one with a defined composition, usually manufactured.
A drug is a chemical used as medicine or taken for its effect. Not all chemicals are drugs.

entry_json.avoid: Note the pronunciation: the ch is a /k/ sound, and the stress is on the first syllable.

entry_json.definition: the front upper part of the body, between the neck and the stomach
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He went to the doctor with chest pain and was sent straight to hospital.
example_sentences: I felt a tightness in my chest after running.
The X-ray showed nothing wrong with his chest.

contexts.text: Chest infections rise every winter in housing that cannot be heated properly.
I had a chest infection for about three weeks last winter.
Chest measurements were recorded for all participants.

confusables.difference: Chest is the neutral anatomical word for everyone. Breast is used in specific medical phrases such as breast cancer.

entry_json.avoid: Chest also means a large strong box. Context makes it obvious, but do not mix the two in one sentence.

entry_json.definition: most important, or highest in rank
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chief advantage of the scheme is that it costs almost nothing to run.
example_sentences: Poor housing is the chief cause of the problem.
She is the chief executive of a small charity.

contexts.text: The chief obstacle to reform is not public opinion but the cost of the transition.
The chief reason I moved was the cost of living.
The chief limitation of the study is its small sample.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning, but chief is more formal and appears more in written argument than in speech.
Principal is equally formal and slightly more common in academic writing. Both are safe alternatives to main.

entry_json.avoid: Chief goes before a noun only. Do not write the reason is chief.

entry_json.definition: the period of your life when you are a child

Childhood obesity has risen steadily for twenty years.

contexts.text: Childhood obesity rates have doubled in two decades, and school meals are only part of the explanation.

Childhood exposure to lead was associated with lower test scores.

confusables.difference: Youth covers the teenage years and early twenties. Childhood ends before that.
Upbringing is how your parents raised you. Childhood is simply the period of time.

entry_json.avoid: Childhood is usually uncountable: during childhood. It takes an article only with an adjective: a happy childhood.

entry_json.definition: the facts or conditions surrounding an event, which affect what happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Under normal circumstances the process takes about a month.

contexts.text: Children who succeed despite difficult circumstances are often held up as proof that circumstances do not matter.
Under the circumstances, I think they handled it well.
Participants' economic circumstances were recorded at the outset.

confusables.difference: Situation is the state of affairs as a whole. Circumstances are the particular conditions that shaped it.

entry_json.avoid: Usually plural. Under the circumstances or in the circumstances are both correct; under no circumstances is emphatic and takes inversion.

entry_json.definition: to mention something as a reason or example, or to refer to a source in academic writing

They cited health reasons, but nobody really believed that.
The paper has been cited over two thousand times.

confusables.difference: Quote means repeating someone's exact words. Cite means referring to a source or giving something as a reason, without necessarily quoting.

entry_json.avoid: Cite is one of the strongest Task 2 verbs: the reason most frequently cited is. Do not confuse the spelling with site.

Ordinary citizens had no say in the decision.

My grandfather became a citizen here in the nineteen sixties.
Citizens aged over 65 were surveyed separately.

confusables.difference: A resident lives somewhere but may hold another nationality. A citizen has legal nationality and the rights that come with it.

entry_json.avoid: Senior citizen is a polite phrase for an older person. Citizen alone never means a city dweller in modern English.

entry_json.definition: connected with the ordinary people of a country rather than the military or religious authorities
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Civil servants implement the policies that ministers announce.
example_sentences: The country suffered a long civil war.
Civil rights were extended only gradually.

contexts.text: Civil society organisations often deliver services more cheaply than either government or business.

Civil conflict was recorded in eleven of the countries studied.

entry_json.definition: to say something is true without proving it; also to formally ask for something you are entitled to
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The company claims its packaging is fully recyclable, which is not quite true.

You can claim a refund within thirty days.

The authors claim that the effect persists over five years.

entry_json.avoid: Claim quietly tells the reader you do not believe it. Do not use it about facts you accept.

entry_json.definition: typical of its kind, or of lasting quality and widely admired
entry_json.own_context_sentence: That is a classic example of a policy solving one problem and creating two more.

He made the classic mistake of revising only what he enjoyed.

contexts.text: This is a classic case of a technology outrunning the law that should govern it.
It is a classic tourist trap, but I still enjoyed it.
The paper is now regarded as a classic study in the field.

confusables.difference: Classical refers to ancient Greece and Rome, or to a style of music. Classic means typical or of lasting quality. They are not interchangeable.

entry_json.avoid: Classical music, but a classic film. Writing classical film is a very visible error.

entry_json.definition: a group of words with a subject and a verb; also a section of a legal document
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
example_sentences: The contract has a clause about early cancellation.
Try joining the two clauses with although.

Relative clauses were coded separately in the analysis.

confusables.difference: A sentence can contain several clauses. A clause is the smaller unit built around one verb.

entry_json.avoid: Clause is pronounced /klɔːz/, identical to claws. Do not confuse it with cause /kɔːz/.

entry_json.definition: to press a button on a computer mouse, or to make a short sharp sound
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Click on the link at the bottom of the page to confirm.
example_sentences: The door clicked shut behind us.
Just click here and the form opens.

contexts.text: Designers deliberately make the button you should not click harder to find.
You just click on that and it downloads automatically.
Click-through rates were recorded for each version of the page.

confusables.difference: You press a physical button or a key. You click a mouse or a link on screen.

entry_json.avoid: Click ON a link, or simply click the link. Both are correct; click to a link is not.

entry_json.definition: a person or organisation that pays for professional services
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of our clients are small businesses.

She meets clients three or four times a week.

contexts.text: Professional services firms compete for a small number of large clients, which makes them fragile.

Client satisfaction was measured through an annual survey.

confusables.difference: A customer buys goods in a shop. A client pays for a professional service: legal, financial or design work.

entry_json.avoid: Shops have customers; lawyers and accountants have clients. Choosing the wrong one is immediately noticeable.

entry_json.definition: in a way that involves careful attention, or with a strong connection

example_sentences: Look closely at the second paragraph.
The team worked closely with local residents.

contexts.text: Income and life expectancy are closely linked, though the relationship is not a simple one.
I work quite closely with two other people on that project.
The observed pattern closely matches the model's prediction.

entry_json.definition: material made from cotton, wool or a similar substance; also a piece of it used for cleaning
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wipe the surface with a damp cloth.
example_sentences: The bag is made of a heavy cotton cloth.
She put a clean cloth on the table.

contexts.text: Replacing paper towels with washable cloth cuts household waste noticeably.
I keep a cloth by the sink for wiping things down.
Cloth production accounted for a third of exports in 1850.

entry_json.avoid: Cloth is uncountable for the material: some cloth. Clothes is always plural: my clothes are, not my clothes is.

entry_json.definition: a piece of information that helps you solve a problem or answer a question
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The graph gives a useful clue about why sales fell.
example_sentences: Police found no clues at the scene.

contexts.text: Fossil records provide the only clues we have about how quickly earlier climates changed.
I had absolutely no clue what he was talking about.
Contextual clues helped readers infer unfamiliar vocabulary.

entry_json.avoid: I have no clue is informal. In writing use there is no evidence or it is unclear.

entry_json.definition: a hard black substance dug from the ground and burned to produce heat

Burning coal produces more carbon dioxide than any other fuel.

Coal accounted for 60 per cent of electricity generation in 1990 and 12 per cent by 2020.

entry_json.definition: a small flat piece of metal used as money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fewer people carry coins now that most payments are by card.
example_sentences: I found an old coin under the floorboards.
The machine only takes coins.

Coins recovered from the site date from the third century.

entry_json.definition: to fall down suddenly, or to fail completely

entry_json.definition: a group of similar things kept or brought together; also the act of collecting something

I have a small collection of postcards from everywhere I have been.
Data collection took place between March and June.

confusables.difference: A group can be people or things gathered by chance. A collection is deliberately assembled and usually kept.

entry_json.avoid: Data collection, waste collection and rubbish collection are fixed compounds and take no article.

entry_json.definition: having a particular colour, or having colour rather than being black and white
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart uses coloured bars to distinguish the three regions.
example_sentences: She handed out coloured pencils to the class.
Brightly coloured packaging attracts younger buyers.

contexts.text: Brightly coloured packaging aimed at children should be restricted for high-sugar foods.
The walls are painted quite a bright colour, which I like.
Coloured markers indicate the three experimental conditions.

confusables.difference: Colourful means having many bright colours and is a compliment. Coloured just means it has some colour.

entry_json.avoid: Never use coloured about a person. It is offensive and dated in British English. Say Black, or people of colour if you need the term.

entry_json.definition: two or more things joined or used together, and the result of doing so

The colour is a combination of blue and grey.

contexts.text: The improvement resulted from a combination of investment, regulation and simple public pressure.
It was a combination of things, really, not one single reason.
The two treatments were most effective in combination.

entry_json.avoid: A combination OF things, or in combination WITH something. Not a combination between.

entry_json.definition: to join two or more things together so they work as one
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many students combine full-time study with part-time work.
example_sentences: The course combines theory and practical experience.
Combine the flour and the water before adding anything else.

contexts.text: Policies that combine higher fuel taxes with better public transport succeed where either alone would fail.
I combine work and study, which is exhausting but worth it.
The two datasets were combined before analysis.

confusables.difference: Mix implies stirring things into one substance. Combine keeps the elements working together but distinct.

entry_json.avoid: Combine A WITH B, or combine A AND B. Not combine A to B.

entry_json.definition: the state of being physically relaxed and free from pain or worry; also something that makes you feel better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The seats are designed for comfort rather than for fitting more people in.
example_sentences: You can watch it from the comfort of your own home.
It was some comfort to know that others had failed too.

contexts.text: Modern housing is built for comfort, and comfort now accounts for a large share of household energy use.
I value comfort over style when it comes to shoes.
Thermal comfort was assessed using a standard questionnaire.

confusables.difference: Comfort is the noun, comfortable the adjective. Travel in comfort, or a comfortable journey.

entry_json.definition: an order given to someone; also control over people or a good knowledge of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She has an excellent command of three languages.
example_sentences: The officer gave the command to advance.
The general took command of the region in 1943.

contexts.text: A good command of English is now expected in professions that never required it a generation ago.
I would say I have a reasonable command of French, but not much more.
Voice commands were recognised correctly in 94 per cent of trials.

confusables.difference: An order is the everyday word for telling someone to do something. Command is military or technical.

example_sentences: Consumer spending fell for three consecutive quarters.
The law protects consumers from misleading advertising.

contexts.text: Consumers say they will pay more for sustainable products, and then reliably choose the cheaper option.
As a consumer I do look at where things are made now.
Consumer confidence declined steadily throughout 2008.

confusables.difference: A customer buys from one specific shop or company. A consumer is anyone who uses goods, considered as a group in economics.
Clients pay for professional services. Consumers buy products.

entry_json.avoid: Consumer is the word for essays about economics and advertising. Customer is the word for a specific transaction.

entry_json.definition: communication with someone, or the state of touching something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am still in contact with two people from that course.
example_sentences: Please give a contact number on the form.
Avoid contact with the eyes.

contexts.text: Regular contact with the wider family protects older people from isolation more effectively than any service.
I am still in contact with my best friend from school.
My contact details are given at the end of this letter.

confusables.difference: Communication is the process of exchanging information. Contact is simply being in touch, however briefly.
Connection is a link between things. Contact is between people.

entry_json.avoid: In contact WITH someone. Get in contact, keep in contact and stay in contact are all correct; make contact is for the first time.

entry_json.definition: a box, bottle or similar object used for holding something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reusable containers cut a surprising amount of household waste.
example_sentences: Store the leftovers in an airtight container.
The port handles thousands of containers a day.

contexts.text: Charging for single-use containers reduced their use by more than eighty per cent within a year.
I take my own container to the market, which saves a lot of plastic.
Containers were sealed and stored at a constant temperature.

confusables.difference: Packaging is the material wrapped around a product for sale. A container is the object that holds things, and is usually reusable.
A box is one kind of container, made of card or wood. Container is the general term.

entry_json.avoid: Container is countable. In shipping it means the large steel unit, which is a useful Task 1 vocabulary item.

entry_json.definition: a competition in which people try to win something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The contest attracted entries from over thirty countries.
example_sentences: She won a writing contest at fifteen.
The election turned into a two-way contest.

contexts.text: Turning school achievement into a contest motivates the strongest students and discourages everyone else.
I entered a photography contest once and came nowhere.
The contest between the two candidates was decided by fewer than 500 votes.

confusables.difference: Competition is the more common British word for the event and also names the activity in general. Contest is slightly more formal or literary.
A match is between two teams or players in sport. A contest can have many entrants and need not be sporting.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is /ˈkɒntest/ with front stress; the verb, meaning to dispute or challenge, is /kənˈtest/.

entry_json.definition: happening without stopping or without any break
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The machine emits a continuous low noise.
example_sentences: There has been continuous growth for six years.
Continuous assessment replaced the final exam.

contexts.text: Learning a language is a continuous process rather than a course you finish.
There is a continuous hum from the fridge that I only notice at night.
The line shows continuous growth from 1995 to 2015.

confusables.difference: Continuous means with no break at all. Continual means repeated with gaps, often annoyingly. Rain can be continuous; interruptions are continual.
Constant emphasises not changing in amount. Continuous emphasises not stopping in time.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, continuous growth means the line never falls. If it dips, write overall growth instead.

entry_json.definition: a formal written agreement that is legally binding
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I signed a twelve-month contract before I read all of it.
example_sentences: The company won a contract to supply the schools.
Read the contract carefully before you sign.

contexts.text: Short fixed-term contracts give employers flexibility and give workers no way to plan their lives.
My contract runs out in June, so I am looking around already.
Workers on temporary contracts reported lower job satisfaction.

confusables.difference: An agreement can be informal or spoken. A contract is written and legally enforceable.
Deal is the informal word for the commercial arrangement. Contract is the document that records it.

entry_json.avoid: The noun is /ˈkɒntrækt/ with front stress; the verb meaning to shrink or to catch an illness is /kənˈtrækt/.

entry_json.definition: a clear difference between two things when they are compared
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a sharp contrast between the two halves of the city.
example_sentences: In contrast, spending on transport fell every year.
The contrast between the figures is striking.

contexts.text: In contrast, the rural figure barely changed over the entire period.
The contrast between the two cities was quite a shock at first.
There is a striking contrast between what people say about recycling and what they do.

confusables.difference: A comparison looks for both similarities and differences. A contrast points only at the differences.
Difference is the plain noun. Contrast implies the difference is large and immediately visible.

entry_json.avoid: In contrast and by contrast both start a sentence. In contrast TO or WITH something. Not in contrast of.

entry_json.definition: to give money, help or ideas towards something; also to be one of the causes of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Traffic contributes more to urban air pollution than industry does.
example_sentences: Everyone contributed something towards the gift.
Several factors contributed to the decline.

contexts.text: Deforestation contributes significantly to emissions, yet receives a fraction of the attention given to transport.
We all contributed a bit towards the cost of the trip.
Three variables contributed significantly to the model.

confusables.difference: Cause claims full responsibility. Contribute to says it is one factor among several, which is usually the more defensible claim.
Donate is only about giving money or goods to a cause. Contribute also covers ideas, effort and causal influence.

entry_json.avoid: Contribute TO something. The stress is on the second syllable: /kənˈtrɪbjuːt/.

entry_json.definition: something you give or do to help achieve something, or an amount of money given
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Her contribution to the project was far larger than the credit she received.
example_sentences: Small daily changes make a real contribution over a year.
Employers pay a contribution towards the pension.

contexts.text: Individual behaviour makes a real contribution, but it cannot substitute for regulation.
I would like to think I made some contribution to the team.
Each factor's contribution to the total variance is shown in Table 3.

confusables.difference: A donation is money or goods given to a charity. A contribution can be effort, ideas or part of a shared cost.
Participation is taking part. A contribution is what you actually add.

entry_json.avoid: Make a contribution TO something. Not do a contribution, and not contribution for.

entry_json.definition: useful because it saves you trouble, or easy to reach and use
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flat is convenient for the station, which is why we took it.
example_sentences: Would Thursday be convenient for you?
Online banking is more convenient but less secure.

contexts.text: Online shopping is convenient for the customer and expensive for the environment.
My flat is really convenient for work, about ten minutes on foot.
Please let me know a convenient time to discuss the matter.

confusables.difference: Comfortable is about physical ease. Convenient is about saving time and effort. A long train journey can be comfortable but inconvenient.
Suitable means right for the purpose. Convenient means it fits easily into your arrangements.

entry_json.avoid: Convenient FOR a place or a person, and convenient TO DO something. Never convenient of.
